title: UH-60M Black Hawk

sources.title: JoyPro cockpit catalog (panels, items and grip functions of the variant)
TM 1-1520-237-10 Operator's Manual UH-60A/L (US Army, public domain)

intro: The UH-60M is the modernised Black Hawk of the 2000s: stronger engines run by FADEC computers, new rotor blades and a glass cockpit with four screens, and a digital flight control system that can fly coupled approaches. The roof panel with the engine levers and fire handles stays much as in the UH-60A/L, and JoyPro takes the grips as unchanged, so this guide builds on the UH-60A/L guide. The extra switches of the M's flight director are not described in the sources JoyPro uses.

panels.name: Overhead console
panels.text: The roof panel with the engine power and fuel levers, the engine fire handles, the starters, the APU and the electrical, anti-ice and lighting panels.
panels.context: The whole start-up happens here, from the battery to the engine levers; the fire handles are where both pilots can reach them.

controls.name: ENG POWER CONT levers

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: Fuel to the engine is shut off.

positions.name: IDLE
positions.text: Position for the start and for idling on the ground.

positions.name: FLY
positions.text: The engine control keeps the power turbine at its normal speed.

positions.name: LOCKOUT
positions.text: The automatic engine control is bypassed; the pilot sets the power by hand.

controls.text: Two levers, one for each of the two engines. They give each engine fuel and decide its power setting, from off through idle to the flying position.
controls.context: In the UH-60M a FADEC (a computer that runs each engine by itself) governs the engines when the levers are in FLY; the pilot moves them during the start and the shutdown.

controls.name: ENG FUEL SYS selector levers

positions.name: DIR
positions.text: The engine is fed from its own tank.

positions.name: XFD
positions.text: The engine is fed from the other tank (crossfeed).

controls.text: One lever per engine that chooses where its fuel comes from: off, direct from its own tank, or crossfeed (from the other side's tank).
controls.context: Crossfeed keeps an engine running when its own tank or fuel line has a problem.

controls.name: ENG EMER OFF T-handles
controls.text: One T-shaped handle per engine. Pulling it shuts off the fuel to that engine and arms the fire extinguisher; a FIRE light in the handle shows a fire.
controls.context: It is the first step when an engine burns; the bottle is then fired with the FIRE EXTGH switch.

controls.name: FIRE EXTGH switch
controls.text: This switch fires a fire extinguisher bottle into the engine whose T-handle was pulled: the main bottle or the reserve bottle.
controls.context: The reserve bottle is for a fire that the main bottle did not put out.

controls.name: ENG 1 / ENG 2 starter buttons
controls.text: One button per engine that starts its air starter, which spins the engine with air until it can run on its own.
controls.context: The air comes from the APU; the engines are started one after the other with the power lever at IDLE.

controls.name: APU control
controls.text: The switches that start and run the APU (a small extra engine that makes electricity and air before the main engines run) and put its generator on line.
controls.context: The APU is started first; it powers the cockpit and gives the air for the engine starters. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Electrical power panel
controls.text: Switches for the helicopter's electricity: BATT, GEN 1, GEN 2 and APU GEN. The battery stores electricity for when the engines are off; generators make electricity while the engines run.
controls.context: They are among the first switches the pilot uses when climbing in, because almost every other system needs electricity. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Fuel pump switch

positions.name: FUEL PRIME
positions.text: Fills the fuel lines for the start.

controls.text: This switch runs a fuel pump: FUEL PRIME fills the fuel lines before the start, APU BOOST helps feed fuel to the APU.
controls.context: It is used in the start-up before the APU and the engines are started.

controls.name: Anti-ice and lighting panels
controls.text: Switches for the engine anti-ice (keeps ice out of the engine air intakes), the pitot heat (heats the tubes that measure speed) and the outside and cockpit lights.
controls.context: Anti-ice is switched on in cold, wet air; the lights are set before a night flight. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

areas.name: Instrument panel
areas.text: The four screens and the standby display.

panels.name: Instrument panel (glass cockpit)
panels.text: Four colour screens, two for each pilot, a standby instrument and the master warning lights.
panels.context: The UH-60M replaced the round dials and light columns of the A and L with these screens, which show the flight and the engine data on pages.

controls.name: Pilot MFDs (2)
controls.text: The pilot's two colour screens (multi-function screens with buttons around their edge). They show the flight instruments, the navigation map and the engine pages.
controls.context: Instead of dozens of round dials, the crew picks the page each screen shows; one screen can replace another that fails.

controls.name: Copilot MFDs (2)
controls.text: The copilot's two colour screens (multi-function screens with buttons around their edge). They show the same pages for the other seat, so either pilot can fly.
controls.context: One pilot usually flies while the other works the map, the radios and the systems.

controls.name: MFD bezel keys
controls.text: Buttons around the edge of each screen. Each one picks the word printed next to it on the screen, so the same button does different things on different pages.
controls.context: The crew uses them to change pages and options; the page layout is not described in the sources JoyPro uses.

controls.name: Standby flight display
controls.text: A small separate instrument that shows the attitude (nose up or down, leaning left or right), the speed and the height. It keeps working when the big screens fail.
controls.context: It is the backup that lets the pilot fly safely to a landing if the main displays go dark.

controls.name: Master warning / caution lights
controls.text: Two big lights: master warning means "danger now", master caution means "something needs your attention". The message on the display says what is wrong.
controls.context: Pressing the light usually acknowledges it, so it is ready to show the next problem.

areas.name: Centre console
areas.text: Flight management keypads, flight control panel and backup radios.

panels.name: Centre console
panels.text: The console between the seats with two keypads for the flight management system, the flight control panel, backup radio controls and the countermeasures.
panels.context: With the glass cockpit most settings are typed into the flight management system instead of turned on separate radio boxes.

controls.name: Control display units (2)
controls.text: A keypad with a small screen where the crew types the route, the radio frequencies and other flight data for the flight management system (the computer that plans and follows the route), like a small computer keyboard.
controls.context: The crew sets up the route and the radios with it before the flight and changes them in flight. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: AFCS / flight director panel
controls.text: Buttons that switch on and off the stability helpers, the trim, the coupled modes (where the autopilot flies a course by itself) and the flight director (steering marks for the pilot). Stability helpers keep the helicopter steady and smooth; the autopilot can hold height, heading or speed so the pilot does not have to.
controls.context: The helpers stay on for almost the whole flight; the pilot switches them off only for tests or when one fails. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Radio control panels
controls.text: Backup controls for the radios, used when the radios cannot be set through the keypads.
controls.context: Normally the crew tunes the radios through the flight management system. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Countermeasures control
controls.text: The switches that arm the dispensers of countermeasures, things the helicopter throws out to fool enemy missiles: chaff (clouds of metal strips for radar missiles) and flares (hot burning decoys for heat-seeking missiles). It also controls the CMWS, a system that sees approaching missiles and warns the crew.
controls.context: They are armed after take-off and made safe before landing, so nothing fires on the ground. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.
